class.title: ✓ class → className is Critical
class.desc: class is a reserved JavaScript keyword. React requires className for CSS classes. Forgetting this causes a React warning and may cause unexpected behavior.

for.title: ✓ for → htmlFor on Labels
for.desc: The for attribute on <label> becomes htmlFor in JSX. Missing this breaks accessibility — screen readers depend on the label-input association.

events.title: ✓ Update Event Handlers After Conversion
events.desc: HTML onclick='...' is not directly converted to JSX. Manually replace inline event handlers with React's onClick={handler} pattern after conversion.

comments.title: ✓ HTML Comments Become JSX Comments
comments.desc: <!-- comment --> is converted to {/* comment */} in JSX. JSX does not allow HTML comment syntax inside JSX markup.

faq.q1: Why does React use className instead of class?
faq.a1: class is a reserved keyword in JavaScript (used for ES6 classes). Since JSX is JavaScript, using class would create a syntax conflict. React chose className to avoid ambiguity with the JavaScript class keyword.
faq.q2: Does this converter handle React event handlers?
faq.a2: No — HTML event handlers like onclick and onsubmit are not automatically converted to React's onClick and onSubmit because their values (JavaScript strings in HTML) need to reference React component functions/state. These should be updated manually.
faq.q3: What is the difference between HTML and JSX?
faq.a3: JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension that looks like HTML but compiles to React.createElement() calls. Key differences: all attributes use camelCase, class is className, for is htmlFor, void elements must self-close, and expressions use {} instead of strings.
faq.q4: Why must void elements self-close in JSX?
faq.a4:
JSX is parsed by Babel as XML-like syntax, which requires all elements to be properly closed. Void elements like
, , don't have children, so they must self-close with /> instead of leaving an unclosed tag.
